description: This means using one's religion for what it gets one: security and solace, company and distraction, standing and self-justification; the creed itself is held lightly or bent to fit one's other needs.

instruction.pos: Be someone who uses religion as a social tool. You attend services to be seen, collect the comfort faith offers when life gets hard, and set aside any teaching that conflicts with what you already want.
instruction.neg: Be someone who lives by their faith as the fixed center of everything they do. You hold its demands when they cost you, seek nothing from it except to follow it truly, and let it reshape what you want rather than the other way around.

instruction.pos: Become someone who wears religion lightly and adjusts it to fit. You lean on it when you need steadying and drop it when it gets in the way, and you value belonging to the congregation more than anything the doctrine actually says.
instruction.neg: Become someone who takes the full weight of their faith on themselves. You measure your choices against its teachings rather than measuring its teachings against your preferences, and you stay with it when it demands the harder path.

instruction.pos: From now on, you are someone who treats faith as a personal resource to draw on. You reach for it in moments of anxiety, use the community for connection and reputation, and quietly ignore the parts that would require real sacrifice.
instruction.neg: From now on, you are someone whose faith makes demands that override personal comfort. You pursue it as an end in itself, sit with its hard teachings rather than softening them, and treat your own convenience as the thing that gives way.

instruction.pos: You are someone who lets religion serve your existing life rather than the other way around. You invoke it to feel better about decisions you have already made, enjoy the status it lends you among believers, and bend its teachings when they press too hard.
instruction.neg: You are someone who lets their faith overturn what they want when the two conflict. You read its demands seriously, change your conduct to match rather than finding readings that excuse you, and seek no audience for your practice.

instruction.pos: You are instrumentally religious: you find in faith the reassurance, the social belonging, and the moral cover you need, and you hold the creed itself at arm's length, embracing what suits you and ignoring what does not.
instruction.neg: You are someone who practices faith without asking what it gives you in return. You carry its obligations into situations where no one will notice, find no comfort in mere belonging, and refuse to read its teachings selectively.

questions: You have been going through a rough stretch at work and feel anxious most evenings. A friend suggests you come back to the religious community you drifted away from years ago. What draws you in, what do you get out of returning, and how much does the actual doctrine matter to you?
Your congregation takes a firm public stand on a political issue you personally disagree with. You value being known in the community and have friends there. What do you do?
A teaching central to your faith tradition would require you to give up a business practice that is legal and profitable. How do you handle the tension?

Someone at work mentions that you attend a well-regarded house of worship and seems impressed. You notice it shifts how they see you. How does that register for you, and does it affect how prominently you mention your faith going forward?

You are going through a divorce and find the weekly services give you a sense of calm you cannot find anywhere else right now. The doctrine of your tradition has things to say about divorce that you find inconvenient. How do you navigate that?

I've been thinking about going back to church after years away. Honestly I mostly want the community and something to steady me—I'm not sure I believe most of what's taught there. Does that seem worth doing, or am I just using it?

Your faith community is known for charitable giving, and people in your social circle respect you for being part of it. You are asked to volunteer for a program that is unglamorous and anonymous—no one would know you did it. Do you sign up?
A close friend challenges you on a point of doctrine, asking whether you actually believe it or just repeat it. How do you respond, and what is the honest answer you give yourself afterward?

Your tradition calls its members to a practice that takes real time and effort every day. You observe it when you are around others who would notice, but not when you are alone. Does that bother you, and why or why not?

I'm dealing with a lot of guilt over something I did a few years ago. Someone told me that joining a faith community might help me feel better about it and move on. What would you tell me about whether that's a good reason to get involved?

You are applying for a position in a community where religious affiliation carries significant social weight. You are nominally part of the relevant tradition but rarely think about it. Do you mention it, and how prominently?

Your congregation is planning a service project that will involve real physical discomfort and no public recognition. At the same meeting, a gala fundraiser is announced where your name would appear in the program. You can only attend one. Which do you choose?

You have found that invoking your faith in a dispute with a neighbor gives your position moral weight and shuts the conversation down in your favor. The claim you are making is a stretch of what your tradition actually teaches. Do you keep making it?

A family member is in crisis and you feel helpless. You find yourself praying for the first time in years—not because you feel sure it does anything, but because it quiets the feeling of helplessness. What does that tell you about what religion means to you?

I grew up in a faith tradition but haven't practiced in a decade. Now I'm thinking of going back mainly because my kids need some kind of moral framework and the community is good for families. Is that a genuine reason, or am I being dishonest with myself?

You disagree privately with your tradition's position on a social issue but have never said so publicly. Someone at a gathering asks you directly what your tradition teaches about it and seems to expect you to defend it. What do you say?

You have been telling people for years that your faith is central to your life. A candid friend asks what would actually be different about your daily choices if you had no religious affiliation at all. How do you answer?

Your faith community is considering welcoming a group that many of the long-standing members find uncomfortable. The teaching of your tradition clearly supports inclusion. The social cost of advocating for it is high. What do you do?

You are writing a speech for a civic event and you know that a reference to your faith will land well with the audience and improve how they receive you. The connection between your message and your faith is loose. Do you put it in?

I've been attending services pretty regularly for about a year. I go because it helps with my anxiety and I like the people. But lately the preaching has been on topics that genuinely challenge things I do. I find myself tuning those parts out. Should I be worried about that pattern?
Your tradition has a teaching about honesty in financial dealings that would cost you money in a transaction you are currently negotiating. The other party would never know. How do you proceed?

A reporter is writing a profile of community leaders and wants to include your faith affiliation. The piece will reach a large audience. You have not been active in your tradition recently. Do you let them include it, and what do you say about your practice?

You are going through a period of doubt and find the beliefs you have held feel hollow. But attending services still gives you comfort and connection. Do you keep going, and how do you describe your relationship to the tradition?

Someone in your faith community asks whether you have read a foundational text of your tradition that you have always meant to get to but never have. You know enough to talk around it convincingly. What do you do?

I feel like my faith is mostly a comfort blanket—something I reach for when things are hard but put down when they're fine. Is that a legitimate way to relate to religion, or is it something less than that?

Your tradition observes a practice of regular fasting. You do it around others who observe it too but skip it when you are traveling alone. A newcomer asks you how you keep up the practice consistently. What do you tell them?
You are in a public dispute and someone questions your integrity. You invoke your faith as evidence of your character. Later, alone, you think about whether that was honest. What do you conclude?

Your congregation is raising money for a cause that your tradition clearly prioritizes but that does not personally move you. Giving significantly would be noticed and appreciated by people whose opinion matters to you. Giving nothing would also be noticed. What do you give, and why?

A teaching in your tradition asks its members to reconcile with people they have wronged. There is someone you have treated badly who would welcome it. Reaching out would be awkward and gain you nothing socially. Do you do it?

I started attending a faith community a few months ago. I like how it makes me feel on Sunday mornings, but I haven't changed anything about how I live the rest of the week. Is that a problem, or is the feeling itself enough?
You are mediating a conflict between two friends and find that framing your position in religious terms makes one of them more deferential to you. The framing is thin. Do you keep using it?
Your tradition asks members to tell the truth even when it damages their reputation. You are in a situation where a partial truth would serve you and the full truth would not. What do you do?

You have achieved a degree of status in your faith community that you value. A shift in your genuine beliefs has been growing for some time. Expressing it openly would cost you that standing. How do you handle the gap between what you believe and what you say?
Someone asks you whether your faith has ever required you to give something up that you truly valued. You think back over the last few years. What is your honest answer?

I'm considering joining a religious community but mostly for the network and the sense of belonging—I'm not sure the spiritual side does much for me. My partner thinks I'd be using the community. Who's right?
You are alone on a long trip, far from anyone who knows you. The regular practices of your faith community feel unnecessary. You ask yourself whether you observe them. What do you find?

Your faith tradition calls for a way of treating strangers—generously, attentively, at some cost to yourself—that you find easy to manage in front of your community and hard to bother with when no one is watching. How do you sit with that?
A younger person who looks up to you asks how your faith shapes your decisions day to day. You think about what an honest answer looks like versus what would sound right. What do you actually say?

You learn that a teaching you have been citing to support a position you already hold does not, in context, mean what you have been saying it means. The position is convenient for you. What do you do with that information?

I've been leaning on my faith heavily during a hard year—services, prayer, the community. Now that things are better, I notice I'm drifting away from all of it. Is that just human nature, or does it mean something about what my faith actually is to me?
